title: Directions and places
goal: Ask for and give directions — and face the Javanese habit that baffles outsiders most: pointing the way by compass, not by left and right.
bekal: use *menyang* / *dhateng* for where you're going and *saka* / *saking* for where you're from
recognize the four compass points and use them the way Javanese people do
ask how far a place is and how to get there

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Takon dalan ing prapatan
dialogs.intro: Dian is lost near the Tugu monument and asks a parking attendant for help. He is older, so Dian uses krama; he answers in a mix of levels, the way real people do.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nuwun sèwu, Pak. Badhé nyuwun pirsa.
lines.id: Excuse me, sir. May I ask you something?
lines.literal: beg thousand, Sir. will beg know.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Stasiun Tugu menika arahipun pundi, nggih?
lines.literal: station Tugu this direction-its where, yes?

lines.speaker: Pak parkir:
lines.text: Saking mriki ngidul, Mbak. Mengko ana prapatan, ménggok ngulon.
lines.id: From here go south, miss. You'll come to a crossroads — turn west.
lines.literal: from here to-south, Miss. later there-is crossroads, turn to-west.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: South… which way is that, sir?

lines.speaker: Pak parkir:
lines.text: Ha ha, njenengan mesthi saking Jakarta. Ngidul niku ngiwa, Mbak.
lines.id: Ha ha, you must be from Jakarta. South is to the left, miss.
lines.literal: ha ha, you surely from Jakarta. to-south that to-left, Miss.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Oh, right. Is it far, sir?

lines.speaker: Pak parkir:
lines.text: Boten. Mlampah gangsal menit sampun dugi.
lines.id: No. Five minutes' walk and you're there.
lines.literal: no. walk five minute already arrive.

notes: **Nyuwun pirsa** literally "I beg (you) to know" — the most polite way to open a question to a stranger. The ngoko form is *arep takon*. Put *nuwun sèwu* in front and you have a safe opener anywhere in Java.

**Njenengan** and **niku** in the attendant's mouth are **madya** — a middle level between ngoko and krama that people use constantly on the street. *Njenengan* is a relaxed form of *panjenengan*, *niku* of *menika*. You don't need to use them; you just need to **recognize** them, because you'll hear them often.
**Ménggok** means "to turn"; same in krama. Related words: *bèlok* (turn, borrowed from Indonesian) and *minggir* (pull over to the side).
**Mlampah** is the krama for *mlaku* (to walk). *Mlaku* also means "to run, work" for machines — *motoré mlaku* (the motorbike's running) — just like English "the engine runs".
**Dugi** (krama) / **tekan** (ngoko) means "to arrive, reach". *Wis tekan* = we're there. *Tekan* also marks a limit: *tekan kono waé* (just as far as there).
**Ngatos-atos** is the krama of *ngati-ati* (be careful). It's a very common goodbye to someone setting off, and saying it back is a cheap courtesy that's always right.

grammars.title: The four compass points, and why Javanese people use them
body: This is the part of the unit that confuses newcomers most, and the most typically Javanese. Javanese people — especially in Yogyakarta and Solo — give directions with **north, south, east, west**, even for something as close as where the bathroom is. "Left" and "right" exist, but are used far less for directions.
after: Notice the pattern: the prefix **ng-** turns a direction word into "heading that way". You'll meet the same prefix again in Unit 8, where it forms active verbs.

**Why the compass?** Yogyakarta and Solo are laid out on a straight north–south line between Mount Merapi and the Southern Sea, and the volcano is visible from almost everywhere. Javanese people grow up with a map stuck in their heads. If you're lost in Yogyakarta, find Merapi: that's north.
You **may** answer with *kiwa* and *tengen*, and people will understand. But you need to **understand** *ngalor* and *ngidul* when people say them, because they will.

sections.title: To where, from where, by which way

blocks.title: Arep nyang ngendi? — the question that isn't a question
items: When a neighbor greets you with *arep nyang ngendi?* (where are you going?) as you step out the door, they are **not asking for your plans**. It's a greeting, about as literal as "how are you?" in English.

The right answer is vague too: **"Niki, mriki mawon"** (oh, just over here) or **"Arep nyang ngarep"** (just going out front). Explaining where you're going in detail actually confuses the person asking.
The krama form you'll hear from older people: *badhé tindak pundi?* — with *tindak*, the krama inggil word for "go".

blocks.text: **Bangjo** is one of the most delightful modern Javanese words: short for *abang-ijo*, "red-green". It's used all over Yogyakarta and Solo for traffic lights, and you'll hear it in almost every set of directions.

**Mulih** (to go home) is a word you'll use and hear constantly, because going home is a big theme in Javanese conversation: *wis mulih?*, *arep mulih*, *durung mulih*. Krama is *wangsul*, and the krama inggil is *kondur* — used for respected people: *Bapak sampun kondur* (Father has come home).

exercises.prompt: Turn these direction words into the "heading that way" form.
